title: The law is omitted from interpretive factors

spanish.text: el propósito de la relación, la productividad, la naturaleza de la relación de empleo, la buena fe, los usos y las costumbres del comercio generalmente observadas

officialEnglish.text: what the parties have agreed upon, the purpose of the relationship, productivity, the nature of the work relationship, good faith, and the general practices and customs of the business sector

independentEnglish.text: the relationship's purpose, productivity, the nature of the employment relationship, good faith, and generally observed commercial usages and customs

meaning: The Spanish expressly lists the law as a guide to interpreting an ambiguous employment-contract provision. The corresponding English list omits it. The next sentence extends this instruction to employer policies and rules.
potentialConsequence: An English-only reader might give less express weight to statutory law in a narrow ambiguity dispute. The omission does not permit an employment contract or policy to override mandatory law.
impactReason: Limited potential impact: this changes an express interpretive factor, but general legal requirements and surrounding provisions substantially constrain the possible effect.
initialAssessment: Two investigators and the adjudicator checked the original Spanish PDF page 20 and official English PDF page 26. 'La ley' appears in the Spanish list and has no corresponding phrase in the English list.
criticalReview: The interpretive list is not necessarily exclusive; mandatory law still applies, and nearby English Sections 2.8 and 2.10 explicitly refer to law. No dispute was identified in which this omission changed an interpretation. Confidence is high in the textual omission, medium-low in a possible outcome change, and low in any actual effect.

downstream.summary: No later administrative or judicial reliance on an interpretation excluding law from the listed factors was found in this first review. A targeted case-law and amendment check remains open.

title: Occupational diseases become injuries
meaning: In the Puerto Rico law carve-out for certain temporary assignees from another jurisdiction, the Spanish names workplace accidents or diseases. The English substitutes injuries for diseases.
potentialConsequence: A narrow English-only reading might leave occupational disease outside the local-law carve-out, affecting medical or compensation rights for a temporarily assigned worker. Whether any governing statute could actually be displaced this way remains unresolved.
impactReason: Major potential impact, conditional on a narrower reading: eligibility for occupational-disease protections could materially affect medical care or compensation, even though the affected group is limited.
initialAssessment: Both investigators and the adjudicator visually verified 'enfermedades' in the original Spanish PDF page 22 and 'injuries' in the official English PDF page 29. Disease and injury name different categories in this context.
criticalReview: 'Work-related injury' can sometimes include disease, and the English sentence refers to laws relating to accidents or injuries; a law relating to accidents may also cover disease. Puerto Rico's workers' compensation law may apply independently. The Labor Department's 2019 guide says Puerto Rico law on accidents or illnesses governs these assignments. Confidence is high in the textual substitution, medium in a material divergent reading, and low in actual legal effect.

downstream.summary: No official decision adopting a disease-excluding English reading was found in this first review. The Labor Department's 2019 guide describes the Puerto Rico-law carve-out as covering workplace illnesses. Further review of Act 45 and case law remains open.

citations.label: Labor Department interpretation guide (2019)
citations.note: Section 3.7 discusses temporary assignments and workplace illnesses.

citations.label: State Insurance Fund Corporation rights overview
citations.note: Distinguishes work accidents and occupational illnesses.

title: Existing employees disappear from the accommodation trigger

spanish.text: notifique al patrono, por escrito, su necesidad de acomodo religioso, el patrono tiene la obligación de acomodar razonablemente las prácticas religiosas del individuo.

officialEnglish.text: notifies the employer, in writing, of his need for religious accommodation, the employer shall have the obligation to reasonably accommodate the religious practices of the individual.

independentEnglish.text: notifies the employer in writing of the need for religious accommodation, the employer must reasonably accommodate the individual's religious practices.

meaning: The Spanish notice condition expressly covers both existing and prospective employees. The English sentence names only prospective employees.
potentialConsequence: If the English sentence were read literally and in isolation, an existing employee could appear unable to trigger the general reasonable-accommodation duty by giving written notice. This is a potential reading, not an established legal outcome.
impactReason: Major potential impact: the divergent reading could remove an important employment right and the corresponding employer obligation for existing workers.
initialAssessment: Two independent investigators and an adjudicator visually checked the original Spanish PDF page 22 against the official English PDF page 29. The omission is in the translated sentence, not the Spanish source.
criticalReview: Later English sentences refer to an employee choosing an accommodation and prohibit an employer from refusing an employee's participation in religious services. These support coverage of current workers when the article is read as a whole. The Labor Department's Regulation 8947 and 2019 guide expressly describe coverage of employees and prospective employees. Confidence is high in the textual omission, medium in a materially different whole-article reading, and low in any actual adverse effect.

downstream.summary: No administrative or judicial reliance on an applicant-only English reading was found in this first review. Regulation 8947 and the Labor Department's 2019 guide instead recognize both groups. A broader case-law and amendment search remains open.

citations.label: Labor Department interpretation guide (2019)
citations.note: Chapter 4 discusses both employees and prospective employees.

title: Traveling sales agents become “travel agents”

spanish.text: , vendedores ambulantes y vendedores externos, según dichos términos son definidos mediante reglamento

officialEnglish.text: , peddlers, and outside salesmen as such terms are defined through regulations

independentEnglish.text: , itinerant vendors, and outside salespeople, as defined by regulation

meaning: The Spanish overtime exclusion names traveling sales agents. The English term ordinarily means workers who arrange trips, an occupation different from the commercial sales category defined by regulation.
potentialConsequence: A literal English-only reading could wrongly identify tourism travel agents as exempt from hours and overtime protections or obscure the intended exemption for traveling sales agents.
impactReason: Major potential impact if the ordinary English occupational label were adopted instead of the incorporated regulatory definition: overtime pay and employer liability could differ.
initialAssessment: Both investigators and the adjudicator checked Spanish PDF page 28 and English PDF page 36. Regulation 7082 Article VIII(C) describes the Spanish category through selling and procuring orders away from the employer.
criticalReview: The same statutory clause expressly incorporates regulatory definitions, which strongly limits a legally informed misreading. Whether Regulation 7082 supplied the operative definition in every post-2017 setting remains to be checked. High confidence in mistranslation; low in actual effect.

downstream.summary: No overtime ruling or administrative decision relying on “travel agents” as tourism workers was identified in this first review. Further regulatory-history and case-law review remains.

citations.label: Puerto Rico Regulation 7082
citations.note: Article VIII(C) defines agentes viajeros as a sales occupation.

title: Exactly twelve employees fall on opposite sides of the vacation exception

spanish.text: patronos residentes de Puerto Rico cuya cantidad de empleados

officialEnglish.text: Puerto Rico resident employers who have

independentEnglish.text: Puerto Rico resident employers whose employee count

meaning: Spanish includes employers with exactly twelve employees in the reduced vacation-accrual exception; English excludes them. Each wording recurs in the next sentence.
potentialConsequence: A literal English reading could give experienced workers at an exactly twelve-person employer the general tenure-based vacation accrual rather than the half-day monthly exception in Spanish.
impactReason: Major potential impact: the threshold governs a statutory leave entitlement and corresponding payroll liability.
initialAssessment: Both investigators and the adjudicator checked Spanish PDF page 32 and English PDF page 40. “Does not exceed twelve” means twelve or fewer; “less than twelve” excludes twelve.
criticalReview: The English paragraph later says the exception ends after payroll exceeds twelve, supporting the inclusive boundary. The 2019 Labor Department guide says twelve or fewer. High confidence in the text difference, medium in an English-only divergent reading, low in actual effect.

downstream.summary: No payroll dispute or ruling adopting the English cutoff was found in this first review. The Labor Department guide follows the Spanish inclusive threshold; broader case-law review remains open.

citations.label: Labor Department interpretation guide (2019)
citations.note: Vacation-accrual exception for employers with twelve or fewer workers.

title: The vacation transition changes at exactly 26 weeks

spanish.text: en cada uno de los dos (2) años calendarios consecutivos

officialEnglish.text: on each one of the two (2) consecutive calendar years

independentEnglish.text: in each of two consecutive calendar years

meaning: Spanish requires the employer to exceed twelve workers for more than 26 weeks in each of two years before the small-employer vacation exception ends. English includes exactly 26 weeks.
potentialConsequence: For an employer at exactly 26 weeks in each relevant year, the English reading could end the reduced-accrual exception one calendar year earlier.
impactReason: Limited potential impact: the discrepancy affects a narrow duration boundary, though affected leave accrual can matter to workers and employers.
initialAssessment: Both investigators and the adjudicator checked Spanish PDF page 32 and English PDF pages 40–41. More than 26 is mathematically different from 26 or more.
criticalReview: The Labor Department guide repeats the strict Spanish greater-than threshold. An English reader might treat its phrasing as an approximation, but the numeric boundary itself differs. High confidence in the text; low in actual effect.

downstream.summary: No affected employer or employee was identified in this first review. The Labor Department guide follows the Spanish greater-than rule; broader downstream review remains.

citations.label: Labor Department interpretation guide (2019)
citations.note: Vacation-accrual transition requires more than 26 weeks.

title: Employer notice becomes a filed wage claim

spanish.text: notificación de la deuda de salario al patrono, judicial o extrajudicialmente
, por el obrero, su representante, o funcionario del Departamento con facultad para ello

officialEnglish.text: judicial or extra judicial claim for the wage debt filed
by the worker, his representative or an official of the Department empowered to do so

independentEnglish.text: notice of the wage debt to the employer, in or out of court
, by the worker, representative, or authorized Department official

meaning: To interrupt the one-year wage-claim limitation period, Spanish specifies notice of the debt to the employer; English omits the recipient and uses “claim ... filed.”
potentialConsequence: If “filed” were treated as requiring a formal proceeding, a worker who timely notified the employer informally could lose a wage claim under that English reading.
impactReason: Major potential impact only under the formal-filing reading, because it would restrict an important wage remedy.
initialAssessment: Both investigators and the adjudicator visually checked Spanish PDF page 33 and English PDF page 42. The wording and stated recipient differ.
criticalReview: “Extrajudicial claim” can encompass an informal demand, and “filed” may be loose drafting. The 2019 Labor Department guide treats employer notice as an interrupting act separate from a court action. Confidence is high in the wording difference, medium-low in a legally sustainable formal-filing reading, and low in actual effect.

downstream.summary: No wage case rejecting timely employer notice because it was not formally filed was found in this first review. The 2019 Labor Department guide supports informal employer notice; further case-law review remains.

citations.label: Labor Department interpretation guide (2019)
citations.note: Wage-claim limitations discussion distinguishes court action from notice to employer.

title: Agricultural worker threshold includes exactly half in English

spanish.text: de cuyo salario en su período básico fue pagado por servicios agrícolas

officialEnglish.text: of whose salary in his base period was paid for agricultural services

independentEnglish.text: of base-period pay from agricultural services

meaning: Spanish requires agricultural services to account for more than 50% of base-period pay; English includes exactly 50%.
potentialConsequence: An even split between agricultural and nonagricultural pay could produce a different benefit-schedule classification under the English reading.
impactReason: Limited potential impact: the difference is confined to an exact-half boundary, and no different payable amount for a specific claimant was established.
initialAssessment: Both investigators and the adjudicator checked Spanish PDF page 42 and English PDF page 52. The companion nonagricultural clause uses 50% or more, so the English can overlap at an even split.
criticalReview: The meaning of “agricultural worker” and agency practice may narrow the affected class. Benefit schedules may also coincide in a particular year. Confidence is high in the numeric divergence, low in actual payment effect.

downstream.summary: No claimant or payment difference was identified in this first review. Agency practice and the applicable benefit schedules still require further checking.

title: A dismissal date becomes a complaint filing date

spanish.text: a la fecha de vigencia de la ‘Ley de Transformación y Flexibilidad Laboral’ quedarán sujetas al término de prescripción previamente en vigor.

officialEnglish.text: to the effective date of the ‘Labor Transformation and Flexibility Act’ shall be subject to the statute of limitations previously in effect.

independentEnglish.text: the Act’s effective date remain subject to the former limitations period.

meaning: Spanish preserves the former limitations period for dismissals that occurred before Act 4 took effect; English appears to test when the complaint was filed.
potentialConsequence: A worker dismissed before enactment but filing afterward could lose the longer former filing period under a literal English reading.
impactReason: Major potential impact: the divergence concerns whether a wrongful-dismissal claim is timely.
initialAssessment: Both investigators and the adjudicator checked Spanish PDF page 49 and English PDF page 61. The act being dated shifts from dismissal to filing.
criticalReview: “Discharges filed” is awkward and might be repaired in context as claims arising from earlier dismissals. The Labor Department’s 2019 guide expressly uses the date of dismissal. Confidence is high in the text difference and low in actual adverse effect.

downstream.summary: No lost claim or ruling using the English filing-date condition was identified. Labor Department guidance follows the Spanish dismissal-date rule; further case-law search remains open.

citations.label: Labor Department interpretation guide (2019)
citations.note: Page 153 explains that the dismissal date controls the former period.

title: Medical release becomes hospital discharge

spanish.text: o fuere autorizado a trabajar con derecho a tratamiento

officialEnglish.text: or was authorized to work while undergoing treatment

independentEnglish.text: or authorized to work while continuing treatment

meaning: The Spanish release trigger for a fifteen-day reinstatement-request period is medical release, which need not involve hospitalization. English adds “from the hospital” in Sections 5.1 and 5.2.
potentialConsequence: An outpatient worker could miss or misunderstand the reinstatement deadline under a literal hospital-only English reading, or the deadline could be tied to the wrong event.
impactReason: Major potential impact: the trigger governs the right to request reinstatement after disability.
initialAssessment: The investigators and adjudicator checked Spanish PDF page 52 and English PDF pages 64–65. Section 5.2 repeats the hospital wording without Section 5.1’s alternative authorization-to-work trigger.
criticalReview: “Hospital discharge” could be loose language for medical release. Section 5.1’s separate work-authorization branch covers some workers, but Section 5.2 lacks it. An older official English Act 45 compilation uses “discharged from treatment.” High confidence in the added hospital restriction; low in actual application.

downstream.summary: No agency or court decision applying a hospital-only trigger was identified in this first review. Further review of reinstatement administration and cases remains.

citations.label: Older English Act 45 compilation
citations.note: Section 5-A renders the trigger as “discharged from treatment.”

title: The pretrial conference deadline is reversed

spanish.text: el tribunal celebrará una conferencia con anterioridad al juicio
no más tarde de 30 días después de contestada la demanda

officialEnglish.text: the court shall hold a conference prior to the trial
at least 30 days after the complaint is answered

independentEnglish.text: the court shall hold a pretrial conference
no later than 30 days after the complaint is answered

meaning: The 1976 Spanish sets a latest conference date, while the English sets an earliest date with no outer limit. A conference on day 20 meets the Spanish rule but not the literal English; day 45 does the reverse.
potentialConsequence: The English reading could delay a mandatory pretrial conference and the opportunity for an order securing potential severance and attorney fees. A material impairment of that remedy in a particular case is possible, but no such case was identified.
impactReason: Limited potential impact generally: the difference changes a court timetable rather than the severance entitlement or formula. A substantial delay could have Major consequences if it impaired security or relief in a particular case.
initialAssessment: Two independent investigators and a third adjudicator visually checked the original Spanish archive PDF page 3, printed page 271, and English archive PDF page 3, printed pages 254–255. The English sentence crosses the gutter of the archival spread. The timing terms are opposite.
criticalReview: The statute also permits a court to require a deposit or bond at any stage when an employer may lack assets, mitigating some risk from a delayed conference. An English reader might infer an obvious mistake from the remedial purpose, but “at least” cannot express the Spanish upper bound. This is the original 1976 text; later amendments changed numbering and provisions, so the historic deadline should not be represented as current law.

downstream.summary: A later government Spanish consolidation and a 2016 appellate opinion retain an upper-bound deadline, though they concern amended versions. No judicial or agency reliance on the 1976 English lower-bound wording, delayed conference, denied security, or changed outcome was identified in this first review.

citations.label: Later Puerto Rico government Spanish consolidation
citations.note: Later amended text preserves “no más tarde” orientation; not evidence of the 1976 deadline remaining current.

citations.label: Puerto Rico Court of Appeals opinion (2016)
citations.note: Quotes a then-applicable amended upper-bound conference rule; does not address this translation.

title: Jobs become employees in the wage-reduction test

spanish.text: en las empresas cubiertas por este Artículo.

officialEnglish.text: in the enterprises covered by this Section.

independentEnglish.text: in the enterprises covered by this article.

meaning: The Spanish conditions the Secretary’s authority to reduce the local minimum-wage percentage on a substantial effect on jobs or employment. The English instead refers to substantial effects on employees, a potentially broader test.
potentialConsequence: An English-only reading could allow the percentage reduction on evidence that workers are substantially affected even if jobs are not. This is a possible interpretation, not evidence that the Secretary lowered any wage or that a worker was paid less.
impactReason: Major potential impact: the disputed condition governs authority to lower an otherwise applicable wage floor for local enterprises outside the federal minimum-wage coverage described in this section.
initialAssessment: The investigator and independent reviewer both identified the jobs/employees distinction in their original pages 1–10 reports. The coordinator checked the Spanish scan at PDF page 2, printed page 695, and English PDF page 4. The scan spells “substancialmente”; one research transcription modernized that spelling and was corrected for publication.
criticalReview: “Affect the employees” can also be understood as affecting their continued employment, which would converge with the Spanish. The original Spanish proviso has awkward syntax, but its noun “empleos” is clear. No administrative application, judicial reading, or actual wage effect was established.

downstream.summary: No targeted review of later amendments, administrative practice, or case outcomes has been completed for this historical translation. No actual effect is established.

sources.label: Original English Act 180-1998 translation
sources.note: PDF page 4; the Section 3 proviso begins on PDF page 3.

title: Optional two-month lookback becomes mandatory

spanish.text: un período no mayor de dos (2) meses antes de usarse o pagarse el beneficio.

officialEnglish.text: To such effect, a period which is not greater than two (2) months
before taking or paying this benefit.

independentEnglish.text: For these purposes, a period of no more than two (2) months
before the benefit is used or paid.

meaning: The Spanish allows consideration of a period up to two months when determining the regular workday for using or paying leave. The English states that such a period shall be considered.
potentialConsequence: Where a worker’s regular day varies, a required lookback could affect a leave calculation. Neither version supplies a precise averaging method, and no actual calculation difference has been shown.
impactReason: Limited potential impact: the English changes permission to apparent obligation, while the two-month ceiling and the rule anchoring the regular day to the time of use or payment remain intact.
initialAssessment: The investigator and independent reviewer both identified the may/shall shift in their original pages 1–10 reports. The coordinator visually checked the Spanish scan at PDF page 4, printed page 698, against English PDF page 7.
criticalReview: Spanish “se podrá” does not say who selects the lookback, and the English could be read as requiring consideration only when past workdays are needed to determine the regular day. The available text does not establish a definite amount or direction of any pay difference.

downstream.summary: No targeted review of later amendments, administrative practice, or case outcomes has been completed for this historical translation. No actual effect is established.

title: Discretion to seek an injunction becomes a filing duty

spanish.text: A tales efectos, el Secretario, siempre que fuere de opinión que cualquier patrono esté infringiendo o va a infringir cualquier disposición de esta Ley,
y cualesquiera otros que fuesen necesarios para hacer efectivos los términos de esta Ley.

officialEnglish.text: To such effects, whenever the Secretary believes that any employer is violating or is going to violate any provision of this Act,
or any other remedies that may be needed to enforce the terms of this Act.

independentEnglish.text: For these purposes, when the Secretary believes an employer is violating or will violate any provision of this Act, the Secretary
and any other necessary remedy to enforce the Act.

meaning: The Spanish authorizes the Secretary to seek an injunction when the Secretary believes an employer violates or will violate the Act. The English turns that specific litigation choice into an apparent duty to file.
potentialConsequence: An English-only reader might treat the Secretary’s belief as triggering mandatory court action and challenge a choice not to sue. No such action, agency response, or changed outcome was identified in this review.
impactReason: Major potential impact: the wording changes a specific discretionary enforcement power into an apparent mandatory litigation duty.
initialAssessment: The investigator and independent reviewer separately identified this modal reversal in their pages 11–17 reports. The coordinator visually checked Spanish PDF page 5, printed page 701, and English PDF page 11.
criticalReview: Both versions first impose a general duty to ensure compliance; this may narrow the apparent difference in practical enforcement. The English also omits an explicit subject before “shall file” and allows other remedies. Whether any court would enforce a mandatory-filing interpretation is unassessed.

downstream.summary: No targeted review of later amendments, administrative practice, or case outcomes has been completed for this historical translation. No actual effect is established.

title: Origin becomes birth as a protected ground

spanish.text: por razón de edad avanzada, raza, color, religión,

officialEnglish.text: by reason of advanced age, race, color, creed,

independentEnglish.text: by reason of advanced age, race, color, religion,

meaning: The original Spanish repeatedly names origin as a protected characteristic, including in operative Sections 1 and 2. The English repeatedly substitutes birth, which may be read as a narrower or different category.
potentialConsequence: A narrow English-only reading could leave some ancestry or geographic-origin discrimination outside the named ground, affecting civil or criminal claims. No affected person or decided case was identified.
impactReason: Major potential impact: the wording defines who receives the law’s employment-discrimination protections and related remedies.
initialAssessment: Both original independent Act 100 reports identified the repeated substitution in the title, motives, and Sections 1–2. The coordinator visually checked the two official archive scans and confirmed the Section 1 wording on Spanish PDF page 1 and English PDF page 1.
criticalReview: Historical legal English can use “birth” to refer to family origin, and “social position” may overlap some situations. The review establishes a plausible difference in reading, not a demonstrated gap in legal protection.

downstream.summary: No targeted review of later amendments, administrative practice, or case outcomes has been completed for this historical translation. No actual effect is established.

title: Power to sue becomes power to order payment

officialEnglish.text: of any sum owing to them

independentEnglish.text: of any amount owed to them.

meaning: The Spanish authorizes the Secretary to demand payment through suit on workers’ behalf; the English operative sentence says the Secretary may order payment. The latter could suggest a direct administrative power.
potentialConsequence: An English-only reader might treat the Secretary as able to impose a payment order without first seeking court relief. No such order or changed outcome was found.
impactReason: Major potential impact: the disputed verb could shift the institution empowered to impose a monetary remedy.
initialAssessment: Both original independent Act 100 reports identified the sue/order difference. The coordinator checked Section 4 on Spanish PDF page 2, printed page 302, and English PDF page 2, printed page 286.
criticalReview: The section begins with court jurisdiction, and the next English sentence refers to “any suit so instituted by the Secretary.” These strong contextual cues support a court-action reading despite the isolated verb. No actual direct-order practice is established.

downstream.summary: No targeted review of later amendments, administrative practice, or case outcomes has been completed for this historical translation. No actual effect is established.

title: Costs and fees may be limited to labor unions

spanish.text: En la sentencia que se dictare contra cualquier patrono u organización obrera
se le impondrán a éstos las costas

officialEnglish.text: In any judgment passed against any employer or labor union
the latter shall be imposed costs

independentEnglish.text: In any judgment against an employer or labor union,
those defendants shall be assessed costs

meaning: The Spanish cost provision refers back to both employers and labor organizations. In the English, “the latter” ordinarily singles out the second named class, labor unions.
potentialConsequence: A literal union-only reading could excuse an employer from costs and attorney’s fees while leaving the main discrimination claim and damages intact. No cost award or denial based on this wording was found.
impactReason: Limited potential impact: the possible exclusion affects a supplementary litigation cost remedy rather than the underlying liability rule.
initialAssessment: The independent reviewer discovered the pronoun issue in the original report. The investigator assessed it only in a coordinator-prompted second pass and agreed a narrower English reading was plausible. The coordinator visually checked both official scans.
criticalReview: The English sentence still opens with judgments against either employers or unions, and its syntax is awkward. A reader may reasonably apply costs and fees to both. This is a plausible ambiguity, not an established exclusion.

downstream.summary: No targeted review of later amendments, administrative practice, or case outcomes has been completed for this historical translation. No actual effect is established.

title: Lottery-prize exclusion appears under annuities in English

spanish.text: Premios de la IVU Loto.-Las cantidades o artículos, de cualquier índole, recibidos por concepto de premios de los sorteos realizados como parte del programa de fiscalización del impuesto sobre ventas y uso conocido como “IVU Loto”.

officialEnglish.text: IVU-Loto Prizes.– The amounts or goods, of any type, received on account of prizes from draws held as part of the Sales and Use Tax Oversight Program, known as the “IVU-Loto.”

independentEnglish.text: IVU-Loto prizes.—Amounts or articles of any kind received as prizes from drawings held as part of the sales-and-use-tax oversight program known as IVU-Loto.

meaning: The Spanish makes IVU-Loto prizes a separate item (b)(12) among exclusions from gross income. The English puts the prize clause at (b)(11)(A)(vi), inside a paragraph introduced as excluding amounts “with respect to annuities.”
potentialConsequence: An English-only literal reading might apply the annuities condition to the lottery-prize clause and treat ordinary IVU-Loto prizes as taxable. No affected return, assessment, taxpayer, or court decision was identified.
impactReason: Major potential impact: if that narrower reading were adopted, a stated exclusion from gross income could become unavailable for ordinary lottery prizes. The label describes possible scope, not a demonstrated tax change.
initialAssessment: An investigator and independent reviewer examined the same targeted original-Code page blocks without consulting one another. Both identified the structural placement difference; the investigator held it after reading the whole subsection, while the reviewer recommended publication. The coordinator visually checked Spanish PDF pages 71–72 and English PDF page 86, and checked the English annuities lead-in on PDF page 85.
criticalReview: The English clause expressly names IVU-Loto prizes and describes lottery drawings, which are plainly unrelated to annuities. The subsection-wide opening also lists items excluded from gross income. A reader could treat “(vi)” as an obvious numbering or indentation error and give the prize clause the same standalone effect as Spanish. The original Code already had (b)(11) for annuities in both languages; Act 4’s later severance-numbering history has not been reconstructed.

downstream.summary: The comparison covers selected pages of the original 2011 Code only. Later amendments, tax administration, and actual assessments have not been traced; no real tax consequence is established.
